lead: Multicomponent distillation separates three or more volatile components. Binary McCabe-Thiele no longer works because every component distributes between distillate and bottoms. Shortcut methods give a quick design: choose two key components, use Fenske for minimum stages, Underwood for minimum reflux, and Gilliland for stages at a chosen reflux. These estimates size a column before rigorous computer calculation. Refineries and petrochemical plants use them for LPG recovery, crude fractions and solvent recovery, where a fast first design matters.

sections.h3: Keys turn a multicomponent problem into a key pair

blocks.text: A multicomponent feed has components with different volatilities. The light key (LK) is the more volatile component whose recovery in the distillate you specify. The heavy key (HK) is the less volatile component whose recovery in the bottoms you specify. Components lighter than LK are light non-keys; components heavier than HK are heavy non-keys.

Non-key distribution is the amount of each non-key component that leaves in distillate or bottoms. The shortcut equations below use only the two keys. Estimate non-key distribution separately if needed; it is not part of the key equations.

All shortcut methods assume constant relative volatility α and constant molar overflow (CMO). α<sub>i</sub> is the volatility of component i relative to the heavy key: α<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>HK</sub>, where K<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub> at equilibrium. CMO means liquid and vapour molar flows are constant within each column section. These assumptions make the algebra simple and give a first design, not a rigorous tray-by-tray result.

sections.h3: Fenske: minimum stages at total reflux

blocks.text: At total reflux no product is removed, so the column needs the fewest theoretical stages for a required separation. Fenske gives this minimum stage count N<sub>min</sub> from the key split.
N<sub>min</sub> = log<sub>10</sub>[(d<sub>LK</sub> / b<sub>LK</sub>)(b<sub>HK</sub> / d<sub>HK</sub>)] / log<sub>10</sub> α<sub>LK-HK</sub>
blocks.where: N<sub>min</sub> is the minimum number of theoretical stages; d<sub>LK</sub> and d<sub>HK</sub> are molar flow rates of LK and HK in the distillate; b<sub>LK</sub> and b<sub>HK</sub> are molar flow rates of LK and HK in the bottoms; α<sub>LK-HK</sub> is the relative volatility of LK to HK, taken as a geometric mean if it varies.

blocks.text: Use molar flow rates, not mole fractions, in d and b. If total distillate D and bottoms B are known, d<sub>LK</sub> = D x<sub>D,LK</sub> and b<sub>HK</sub> = B x<sub>B,HK</sub>. A large α<sub>LK-HK</sub> gives a small N<sub>min</sub>. If α<sub>LK-HK</sub> is close to 1, N<sub>min</sub> becomes very large because the keys are hard to separate.
N<sub>min</sub> is not the design stage count. It is the limit at total reflux; the real column runs at a lower reflux and needs more stages.
At minimum reflux the column has a pinch and needs infinite stages. Underwood finds R<sub>min</sub> without stepping trays. First solve the feed equation for θ.

blocks.where: α<sub>i</sub> is the relative volatility of component i to the heavy key; z<sub>i</sub> is the feed mole fraction; q is the feed thermal condition (q = 1 for saturated liquid, q = 0 for saturated vapour); θ is a root lying between α<sub>LK</sub> and α<sub>HK</sub>.

blocks.text: Then use the same θ in the reflux equation.

blocks.where: R<sub>min</sub> is the minimum reflux ratio; x<sub>Di</sub> is the distillate mole fraction of component i; the sum runs over all components.

blocks.text: Use each component's α<sub>i</sub> in both sums. Using only α<sub>LK-HK</sub> for every term is a common error. For a binary key mixture, the equations reduce to the pinch calculation on the y-x diagram.

sections.h3: Gilliland: stages at the chosen reflux

blocks.text: Choose a reflux ratio R above R<sub>min</sub>, often 1.1 to 1.5 times R<sub>min</sub>. Gilliland relates R, R<sub>min</sub>, N and N<sub>min</sub> through two dimensionless groups.

blocks.where: X is the reflux group; Y is the stage group; R is the chosen reflux ratio; N is the theoretical stage count at R.

blocks.text: Read Y from the Gilliland chart or an algebraic fit at the calculated X. Rearrange the definition of Y to get N = (N<sub>min</sub> + Y)/(1 − Y). Then round N up to the next whole number for a stage count.

The result is theoretical stages. N counts the reboiler as one theoretical stage, so the number of trays is about (N − 1)/E, where E is the overall tray efficiency; see 4.7. If R is close to Rmin, X is small and N becomes very large; if R is large, N approaches Nmin.

figure.caption: The shortcut sequence: keys first, then Fenske for minimum stages, Underwood for minimum reflux, Gilliland for stages at the chosen reflux, and finally the rounded actual stage count. Notice that N<sub>min</sub> is not the final count.

examples.question: A binary key mixture has α<sub>LK-HK</sub> = 2.0, distillate LK mole fraction x<sub>D,LK</sub> = 0.98, bottoms LK mole fraction x<sub>B,LK</sub> = 0.02, and saturated-liquid feed with x<sub>F,LK</sub> = 0.50. Find N<sub>min</sub> by Fenske and R<sub>min</sub> by Underwood.
steps: For the binary pair, x<sub>D,HK</sub> = 1 − 0.98 = 0.02 and x<sub>B,HK</sub> = 1 − 0.02 = 0.98. Overall balance gives D/B = (x<sub>F,LK</sub> − x<sub>B,LK</sub>)/(x<sub>D,LK</sub> − x<sub>F,LK</sub>) = (0.50 − 0.02)/(0.98 − 0.50) = 1.00.
Fenske: N<sub>min</sub> = log<sub>10</sub>(49.0 × 49.0)/log<sub>10</sub>(2.0) = log<sub>10</sub>(2401)/0.3010 = 3.3804/0.3010 = 11.23. Report N<sub>min</sub> ≈ 11.2 stages.
At the feed, LK equilibrium vapour mole fraction y* = α x<sub>F</sub>/[1 + (α − 1)x<sub>F</sub>] = 2.0 × 0.50/[1 + (2.0 − 1)0.50] = 0.6667.
Saturated-liquid feed means q = 1. The binary pinch equation gives R<sub>min</sub> = (x<sub>D,LK</sub> − y*)/(y* − x<sub>F,LK</sub>) = (0.98 − 0.6667)/(0.6667 − 0.50) = 0.3133/0.1667 = 1.88.
examples.check:
import math
alpha = 2.0
xD = 0.98
xB = 0.02
xF = 0.50
D_over_B = (xF - xB) / (xD - xF)
ratio_LK = D_over_B * xD / xB
ratio_HK = (1 - xB) / ((1 - xD) * D_over_B)
Nmin = math.log10(ratio_LK * ratio_HK) / math.log10(alpha)
yF = alpha * xF / (1 + (alpha - 1) * xF)
Rmin = (xD - yF) / (yF - xF)
print(f"{Nmin:.1f}")
print(f"{Rmin:.2f}")

traps: Underwood uses each component's α<sub>i</sub>. Fenske needs only α<sub>LK-HK</sub>, which appears in its denominator.
N<sub>min</sub> is the stage count at total reflux, not at the design reflux. R<sub>min</sub> needs infinite stages, not N<sub>min</sub> stages.
The Underwood θ must lie between α<sub>LK</sub> and α<sub>HK</sub> for the key root. A root outside this interval gives a meaningless R<sub>min</sub>.
q is the feed thermal condition, not the reflux ratio. Saturated liquid gives q = 1; saturated vapour gives q = 0.

d and b are molar flow rates, but D and B cancel inside the product (d<sub>LK</sub>/b<sub>LK</sub>)(b<sub>HK</sub>/d<sub>HK</sub>), so Fenske can always be written with mole fractions: N<sub>min</sub> = log<sub>10</sub>[(x<sub>D,LK</sub> x<sub>B,HK</sub>)/(x<sub>B,LK</sub> x<sub>D,HK</sub>)] / log<sub>10</sub> α<sub>LK-HK</sub>. Just do not mix a flow in one factor with a mole fraction in the other.

quiz.q: Define light key and heavy key in multicomponent distillation.
quiz.a: The light key is the more volatile key component whose recovery in the distillate is specified. The heavy key is the less volatile key component whose recovery in the bottoms is specified.

quiz.q: Why is the Fenske stage count called minimum stages rather than design stages?
quiz.a: Fenske applies at total reflux, where no product is removed and separation per stage is largest. A real column runs at a lower reflux and needs more stages.

quiz.q: A binary equimolar feed has α<sub>LK-HK</sub> = 2.5, x<sub>D,LK</sub> = 0.95 and x<sub>B,LK</sub> = 0.05. Find N<sub>min</sub>.
A student uses α<sub>LK-HK</sub> in every term of the Underwood sums. Explain the error.
quiz.a: Each component has its own α<sub>i</sub> relative to the heavy key. The key relative volatility only fixes the interval in which θ lies. Replacing all α<sub>i</sub> by one value destroys the composition dependence and gives a wrong θ and R<sub>min</sub>.

quiz.q: For R<sub>min</sub> = 1.2 and R = 1.8, compute the Gilliland X. If N<sub>min</sub> = 8 and the chart gives Y = 0.45, find N.
What do the constant α and constant molar overflow assumptions mean, and when do they fail?
quiz.a: Constant α means relative volatility does not change with composition or temperature. Constant molar overflow means liquid and vapour molar flows stay fixed in each section. They fail for wide-boiling feeds, large enthalpy changes and strongly non-ideal mixtures.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial flowsheet software solves the rigorous MESH equations for every tray and component. Shortcut methods remain useful for screening options, checking software results and sizing early equipment. Newer work couples them with optimisation and uncertainty analysis for feed changes. Search for rigorous multicomponent distillation, MESH equations, and Inside-Out distillation algorithms.
